subject: literacy
title: Line letters I, L and T

activities.title: Make letters from straight lines
parentPrompts: Show capital I (one standing line), capital L (a standing line and a sleeping line at the bottom) and capital T (a sleeping line across the top, a standing line down the middle).
Build each letter on the table using craft sticks or straws. Name each one.
Then write each on paper. Say the strokes aloud as they go: "down" for standing lines, "across" for sleeping lines.
Ask: "Which letter has just one line?" Look for: they can name I, L and T and write at least one.

subject: literacy
title: Line letters E, F and H

activities.title: More straight-line letters
parentPrompts: Review I, L and T by building one with sticks. Then show capital H (two standing lines with a sleeping line between), E and F.
Build E, F and H with sticks. Ask: "What is the same about E and F? What is different?" (E has one more bar.)
Write each letter on paper with a big pencil or marker, one row each.
Look for: they can tell E from F and know that H has a bar in the middle. Letters do not need to be neat.

activities.title: Skywriting and table writing
materials: a table or a large paper on the floor
parentPrompts: Stand beside your child. Write a letter big in the air with your arm: start at the top, say the strokes aloud.
Have them skywrite the same letter 3 times. Try I, L, T, H, E, F.
Then write the letters with a wet finger on the table or a baking tray. They disappear, so try again freely.
Ask: "Which letter do you want me to guess?" Write one in the air and let them guess. Look for: confident, slow, top-first strokes.

activities.title: Make C and O
parentPrompts: Bend a pipe cleaner into a circle (O) and then open it to make a C. Ask: "What is different?" (C has a gap.)
Trace both letters with a pointer finger, going around the same way each time.
Write a row of O and a row of C. Practice lowercase c and o the same way: they look like small versions.
Look for: the C is open and the O is closed. Name the letters as you go.

activities.title: Write small c, o and a
parentPrompts: Draw a start dot on paper and show how to begin small c at the dot and curve around. Do the same for o.
For small a: draw a small round c shape and then a short standing line on its right side. Go slowly, step by step.
Have your child write a row each of c, o and a. Circle the one they think is best with a highlighter.
Ask: "Which one is your favorite and why?" Look for: letters that stay roughly the same size and start at the top.

activities.title: Number path to 20
parentPrompts: Make a path of 20 squares on the floor or driveway and write the numbers 1 to 20 (adults can write them for the child).
Hop and count together, one number per hop, from 1 to 20.
Now start in the middle: "Start at 7 and keep going." Try starting at 12, then 15.
Look for: counting in order without skipping, and starting from a number other than 1. Stumbles are fine; just count it again together.

activities.title: Count a messy pile
materials: 15 to 20 small things like blocks or buttons
parentPrompts: Spread 12 things out on the table. Ask: "How can we count them so we do not miss any?"
Show the trick: move each counted item from the table into a bowl as you count it.
Let them count a pile of 15, then 18. Count a line of 10 and a circle of 10 too.
Look for: a plan for keeping track, and the right total. Safety: small items are a choking hazard for babies and toddlers, so keep them away from younger siblings and out of mouths.

activities.title: Write numerals in a tray
materials: a baking tray with salt, sand or flour (about half a centimeter deep)
parentPrompts: Write the numeral 1 in the tray with your finger, starting at the top. Let your child copy it.
Do 2, 3, 4 and 5 slowly. Say the number and the amount each time: "3 is this many" (hold up 3 fingers).
Introduce 0: "Zero means none." Put 0 things in the tray. Do 6 to 10 as time allows, on paper or in the tray.
Look for: recognizable numerals. Backward numerals are very common at this age; just show the correct direction and keep going.

activities.title: Compare two groups
materials: about 12 small things like crackers or blocks
parentPrompts: Check for food allergies before using any snack food.
Put 3 things on one plate and 5 on the other. Ask: "Which plate has more? How could we check?"
Match them up one to one, a pair at a time. The extra ones show which has more.
Use the words: more, fewer (or less) and the same. Try 4 and 4, then 6 and 2, then 5 and 3.
Look for: they can pick the plate with more and use the word 'fewer' or 'less' for the other, with matching or counting.

activities.title: Add or take away to make them equal
parentPrompts: Put 4 things on one tray and 6 on the other. Ask: "Are they the same? How can we make them the same?"
Let them try: take 2 from the bigger group, or add 2 to the smaller group. Count to check.
Try a new pair, like 2 and 5. Ask: "Which way do you want to fix it?"
Look for: any workable way to even them. There is more than one right answer.

activities.title: Ask and answer questions
materials: a picture book you have not read yet
parentPrompts: Look at the cover and ask: "What do you think this story will be about?" Read the first few pages.
Pause and ask: "Who is in the story? What did they do?" Let your child answer in a sentence.
Ask your child to ask you a question too. Say: "You are the teacher now."
Look for: they can answer a who/what question and sometimes ask one. Praise questions.

activities.title: Who, where and what happened
materials: a picture book with a clear story
parentPrompts: Read the story. Afterward ask: "Who are the characters? Where does the story happen?"
Ask: "What is one big thing that happens?"
Draw three small boxes on a paper: who, where, what happened. Let them draw in each one.
Look for: they can name a character, a place and an event. Use the pictures to help.

activities.title: Beginning, middle and end
materials: a familiar folktale such as The Three Little Pigs or The Little Red Hen (any telling; the tales are very old and widely retold)
parentPrompts: Read the story or tell it in your own words. Draw three boxes labeled first, next, last.
Ask your child to tell you what happened first. Draw or write a quick note in the first box. Repeat for next and last.
Use the boxes to have them retell the whole story in order.
Look for: events in the right order, with some key details like names of characters.

activities.title: Compare a story and a poem
materials: a short rhyming poem or nursery rhyme from a book (many traditional rhymes are free to use)
parentPrompts: Read a short story. Say: "This is a story. It has characters and things happen."
Read a short poem or a nursery rhyme. Say: "This is a poem. It often has rhymes and a beat." Clap the beat together.
Ask: "Is this one a story or a poem? How can you tell?" Show two short pieces and let them sort them.
Look for: they can tell which one sounds like a poem (rhymes, beat) and which tells a story.

activities.title: Pictures and the story
parentPrompts: Read a page and ask: "What does the picture show that the words do not say?"
Choose a picture and ask: "What moment in the story is this?"
Cover the pictures on one page and ask your child to draw what they think it looks like. Then compare with the real picture.
Look for: they connect a picture to the part of the story it shows.

activities.title: Start a weather chart
materials: paper with 5 boxes (one per day of the week) or a calendar page
a window or a safe spot outside
parentPrompts: Look outside together. Say what you see: sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy. Feel the air outside if safe.
Draw a symbol for today in the first box: a sun, a cloud, raindrops, and so on.
Say: "We will do this every day and look for patterns."
Look for: they can describe the weather in a few words and draw a symbol. Keep the chart for the rest of the unit; add a box each day.

activities.title: Why we check the weather
materials: a weather forecast (from a phone, TV or newspaper)
a few clothes: a rain jacket, a hat, a coat or other
parentPrompts: Look at or listen to a weather forecast for tomorrow. Say: "A forecast tells us what weather may come, so we can be ready."
Ask: "What should we wear if it will rain? If it will be very hot? If it will be cold?" Let them pick clothes.
Dress a toy or draw a person for tomorrow's weather.
Look for: they connect the weather to what to wear or bring, and say why a forecast helps.

activities.title: Look back at the chart
parentPrompts: Look at the chart so far. Count how many days were sunny, cloudy and rainy. Make tally marks.
Ask: "Which was most? Which was least?"
Ask: "What do you think tomorrow will be like? Why do you think so?"
Look for: they can say what happened most often. If you have only a few days, count them. Predictions can be wrong, and that is fine.

activities.title: Helpers in our community
parentPrompts: Ask: "Who helps us in our community?" (a doctor, a bus driver, a teacher, a librarian, a firefighter and many others).
Pick one helper and act out their job. Guess each other's helpers.
Ask: "How does this helper make our day better?"
Look for: they can name a helper and what they do. Include helpers from your own family or neighborhood.

activities.title: Safety rules
materials: a toy car or a pretend street made with tape
parentPrompts: Make a street on the floor. Ask: "What do we do at a crosswalk? In a car? On a bike?" (hold a grown-up's hand, look both ways, wear a seatbelt or helmet).
Act out each safe choice with a toy.
Talk about a rule at a place in your community, like a library (quiet voices).
Look for: they know safety rules and why they matter.

activities.title: Sculpt a letter
parentPrompts: Roll playdough into ropes. Make the first letter of your child's name.
Make another letter from the alphabet in the app.
Decorate the letter with beads or pressed patterns (adult supervision for small items).
Look for: a recognizable letter. Say the sound it makes.

activities.title: Torn paper shapes
parentPrompts: Tear or cut (with safe scissors, adult supervising) paper into shapes: circles, squares and triangles.
Arrange them into a picture of a house, a robot or a bug.
Glue them down. Name the shapes you used.
Look for: they can name some shapes and put them together creatively.

activities.title: Make a beat
parentPrompts: Set up pots and spoons. Show how to play soft and loud.
Play a steady beat while you chant a rhyme.
Switch leader. Ask: "Can you play fast? Slow?"
Look for: they keep a steady beat and try fast and slow. Watch the volume and protect ears.

activities.title: Print with leaves
parentPrompts: Collect a few leaves outside. Wash hands after.
Paint one side of a leaf and press it onto paper.
Print more leaves in different colors.
Look for: they notice the veins on the leaf and the shapes. Do not collect unknown berries or mushrooms.

activities.title: Draw a scene from a story
parentPrompts: Pick a favorite moment from a story you read.
Draw it with the characters and place. Add details.
Tell the story of the picture to you.
Look for: they include a character, a place and an action. Write a title for them.
